metadata.title: Survey of Adult Skills 2023 – Country Notes: Spain

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD country note reports results from the Survey of Adult Skills 2023 (second cycle for Spain) using a household survey design with a personal interview and a self-completed assessment administered on tablets. The note states that the sample was drawn to be representative of the target population of 16-to-65-year-olds in Spain and that analyses were conducted to ensure non-response did not introduce significant bias, but it does not name specific weight variables (e.g., sampling or replicate weights). Because the document is a country results note rather than a microdata analysis paper, it does not provide the exact weighting and variance-estimation variables needed for re-analysis. For any re-use with microdata, analysts should consult the Survey of Adult Skills technical documentation/reader’s companion for the appropriate survey weights and replicate-weight scheme used to produce the reported confidence intervals.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document is a descriptive country note summarising proficiency levels and associations with outcomes; it does not report an empirical predictive model that would require explicit plausible-value (PV) handling or a documented missing-data strategy. The proficiency estimates are presented on 500-point scales with proficiency levels, but the note does not describe whether PVs were used, combined, or how missing responses were imputed. Therefore, PV and missing-data handling details are not available in the provided text, representing a reporting gap for methodological re-use.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The note reports that Spain participated in the Survey of Adult Skills 2023 (2022-23) and that 5,871 adults participated, with a response rate of 61%. It states that the sample was drawn to be representative of about 31.4 million 16-to-65-year-olds residing in Spain, irrespective of nationality, citizenship, or language status. It also explains that some respondents who were not sufficiently fluent could be offered a doorstep questionnaire, and that OECD reports generally exclude doorstep respondents when comparing results across cycles to maximise comparability; the note indicates such exclusions are applied for cross-cycle comparisons.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD country note summarises results from the Survey of Adult Skills 2023 for Spain, covering adults aged 16–65 assessed in three domains: literacy, numeracy, and adaptive problem solving. The assessment was administered exclusively on digital devices (tablets) and proficiency is reported on 500-point scales with discrete proficiency levels; the note reports mean scores, the share of adults at low/high levels, and uncertainty via 95% confidence intervals. For Spain, adults scored below the OECD average in all three domains (literacy 247, numeracy 250, adaptive problem solving 241), with sizable shares at Level 1 or below (literacy 31%, numeracy 30%, adaptive problem solving 35%). The note also describes how skills relate to economic and social outcomes (e.g., employment and labour-force participation, life satisfaction/health, and trust), and how results evolved from 2011–12 to 2022–23, including age-related declines and differences by educational attainment, gender, and immigrant background. It is descriptive and does not provide the microdata ML modelling details (algorithms, PV/missing-data procedures, or weighting variables) needed for causal or predictive interpretation.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is a descriptive OECD country note rather than an empirical ML study: it reports survey-based proficiency distributions and associations using OECD’s published scaling and reporting framework. As a result, there are no model-based ML techniques to extract, no explicit predictive targets with algorithmic performance metrics, and no documented PV/missing-data handling strategy in the provided text. The absence of these fields reflects the document’s purpose (country-level reporting and interpretation) rather than an omission from an ML methodology section.
